title: Mustard greens, fresh, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Mustard greens (Brassica juncea) are edible leafy vegetables commonly used in Asian cuisine. When cooked with added fat, they retain a bright flavor and become tender. They are rich in vitamins A, C, K and minerals such as calcium and iron.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mustard greens belong to the cruciferous family, along with broccoli and cabbage.
The seeds are used to make spicy mustard, while the leaves are enjoyed in salads and side dishes.
In traditional Indian cooking, the leaves are often stir‑fried with oil and spices.
Glucosinolates in mustard greens may support liver detoxification.
Leafy greens lose nutrients quickly during storage, so they are best cooked soon after purchase.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains calcium and iron
items.content: These minerals are important for bones, teeth, and oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Glucosinolates content
items.content: In large amounts they can irritate the gastrointestinal tract in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to mustard greens.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Those prone to kidney stones should consume mustard greens in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The leaves can be quickly stir‑fried in a small amount of oil with garlic, ginger, and soy sauce. They also work well in soups, stews, and mixed vegetable dishes. Freshly prepared greens make a vibrant side for rice or quinoa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh leaves in the refrigerator in a perforated bag with a slight moisture to stay crisp for 3–5 days. Cooked greens with added fat should be eaten within 2 days, stored in an airtight container.
